title: Dark Optical Trapping of Resonant Transition-Metal Dichalcogenide Particles
authors: Patrick Illetschek, Gleb Fedorovich, Albert Seredin, Gleb Tselikov, Valentin S. Volkov, Nikolai Kiesel, Markus Aspelmeyer, Mihail Petrov, Anton V. Zasedatelev
abstract: Mitigating recoil events and minimizing optically induced heating are central challenges in the precise control and cooling of macroscopic particles. To overcome this, we propose trapping resonant dielectric particles for applications in ultra-high vacuum (UHV) levitodynamics. Contrary to other approaches, where suppressing the parasitic resonant scattering was achieved in a standing wave geometry, here we propose a single beam geometry in a dark trap regime. As a promising material platform, we focus on a class of transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) particles with high polarizability, characterized by refractive indices in the range $3.7$-$4.8$ and densities up to $9.3~\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Using full Mie theory, we identify a range of TMD particle radii that support stable axial and radial magnetic quadrupole trapping in a bottle-beam configuration. We predict that for WS$_2$ particles with a mass of $0.5 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{amu}$, one can expect suppression of the scattering rate relative to the mechanical frequency down to $Γ/Ω\simeq 0.02$. This corresponds to a coherence time extended by approximately three orders of magnitude compared with silica particles of the same mass trapped in conventional bright optical traps at UHV. Combined with significantly reduced internal heating, remaining well below the melting point of the material, dark trapping of resonant TMD macroscopic particles emerges as a promising platform for exploring quantum physics with large masses.
summary: The paper proposes using resonant Transition-Metal Dichalcogenide (TMD) particles in a dark optical trap to overcome limitations in cooling and controlling macroscopic objects. By utilizing TMDs' high polarizability and low scattering rates, the authors demonstrate a method that significantly extends coherence time compared to traditional silica traps. This establishes TMDs as a promising platform for quantum physics experiments involving large masses.
main_problem: The central challenge is achieving precise control and cooling of macroscopic particles trapped by light while mitigating detrimental effects like recoil events and optically induced heating.
main_result: Dark trapping using resonant Transition-Metal Dichalcogenide (TMD) particles offers a highly promising platform for levitating large masses with significantly reduced motional decoherence compared to conventional traps.
method: The study employs full Mie theory combined with electromagnetic force calculations derived from the Maxwell stress tensor to model particle trapping in a dark optical trap geometry.
model_or_system: The system involves resonant dielectric TMD particles (like WS2) trapped using a single-beam, 'bottle-beam' configuration operating in an ultra-high vacuum. The analysis models the interaction via multipolar field decomposition near magnetic quadrupole resonances.
key_observables: Suppression of the scattering rate relative to mechanical frequency ($\Gamma/\Omega$), equilibrium temperature ($T_{eq}$), and trapping frequencies (axial vs. radial).
important_parameters: High refractive indices ($3.7-4.8$) and high densities of TMDs; operating wavelength $\lambda_0 = 1550 	ext{ nm}$; low ratio $\Gamma/\Omega \simeq 0.02$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes radiative cooling balances absorption for temperature estimation, but neglects thermo-optical effects like resonance position shifts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dark trap intensity profile (bottle beam), show stable trapping regions dependent on particle radius, and critically compare the low photon recoil ratio ($\Gamma/\Omega$) of TMDs versus high values for silica in bright traps.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the physical challenges (recoil/heating) to proposing the dark trap geometry using TMDs. It then uses Mie theory to calculate trapping forces, analyze stability regions, and quantify improvements in coherence time and thermal management compared to existing materials.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum system dynamics by providing a mechanism (dark trapping with high-density resonators) to extend the coherence time of massive mechanical oscillators interacting with light fields, which is crucial for quantum sensing and measurement.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The dark trap. (a) Normalized EM field intensity in the (xz) plane of the bottle beam formed by two circu- larly polarized Laguerre Gauss (LG) beams with a π phase shift at λ0 = 1550nm; orange arrows indicate force vectors. The beam propagates in the +z direction. The inset shows the force amplitude near the origin, revealing the presence of both a stable and an unstable trapping position. (b) Mul- tipole amplitudes of the field scattered by the particle near the magnetic quadrupole (MQ) resonance. The green-shaded region marks the wavelength range of stable trapping, while the dashed black line shows the trapping beam wavelength.

FIG. 2. Stable trapping conditions. (a) Equilibrium po- sition zeq versus particle radius, normalized to λ0 = 1550 nm. (b) Trap frequencies: axial z (red) and in-plane, radial x, y (blue) for P = 0.80 W. (c) Scattering eﬀiciencies Qscatt of mul- tipoles at zeq for different particle radii: Magnetic quadrupole (MQ), Magnetic Dipole (MD), Electric Dipole (ED), Electric Quadrupole (EQ). (d) Trap depth in units of kBT (T = 300 K), along radial x, y (blue) and axial z (red) directions, for different particle radii. The shaded regions indicate particle radii where no 3D stable trapping is found at λ0 = 1550 nm.

FIG. 3. Photon recoil in the dark trap. Ratio of photon recoil rate to trap frequency, Γ/Ωz, versus particle radius for a WS2 particle in the dark trap (red solid line), with a compen- sating force (red dashed line), for a SiO2 particle of the same radius (black solid line) and of radius 71.5 nm (black dashed line) [2]) trapped in a conventional bright trap. Overlaid are the scattered intensity patterns for particles of different radii.

FIG. 4. Internal heating and thermal emission. (a) Equilibrium temperature Teq versus particle radius for differ- ent extinction coeﬀicients k. The black dotted line indicates the melting point of WS2 at 1520 K. (b) Absorbed power of the trapped nanoparticle. Shaded regions indicate particle radii where stable trapping is not achieved.
